question: Match the device: 50, 51, and 87.
explanation: 50 is instantaneous overcurrent, 51 is time overcurrent, 87 is differential. 86 is the lockout. 27 and 59 are the voltage elements. Learn the numbers; the one-line will not spell them out.
reference: IEEE C37.2 device numbers, as used in ATS 7.9.1 element tests

question: ATS 7.9.1 tells you to determine which of the following on an 87 differential?
choices: Operating-unit pickup, restraint, slope, and harmonic restraint
A 10-minute polarization index of the relay case only
explanation: The 87 list is operating-unit pickup, each restraint unit, slope, harmonic restraint, instantaneous pickup, and the plotted restraint characteristic. The paragraph says to determine harmonic restraint; it does not name the second harmonic in that sentence.

question: Functional checks in ATS 7.9.1 include proving that relay contacts perform which scheme jobs?
choices: Breaker trip, close inhibit, 86 lockout, and alarms
Oil sampling and a turns-ratio test
A Wenner soil box on the station ground
explanation: The functional paragraph names breaker trip tests, close inhibit, 86 lockout tests, and alarm functions, and points at Section 8. A relay that asserts in the test set but never moves the trip wire is not finished.

question: A CT primary is carrying load and someone opens the secondary at the terminal block. The hazard is:
choices: The secondary voltage collapses to zero and is safe to hold
The secondary can develop a dangerous voltage while it tries to maintain ampere-turns
Only the revenue meter is affected; the leads stay at a few volts
The CT automatically shorts itself inside the head
explanation: An open CT secondary with primary current flowing can rise to a hazardous voltage. Short the secondary or leave it on its burden before the primary is energized. ATS also requires exactly one secondary ground, at the place the drawings show.
reference: CT secondary practice; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.9 (one grounding point). Open-circuit voltage is standard CT behavior.

question: You need to see whether an 86 contact is in the breaker close circuit. Which drawing actually shows the coil and the contact?
choices: The one-line, because it shows every contact
The control schematic (or elementary), not the one-line
explanation: A one-line shows the power path and the device numbers. The control schematic shows coils, a and b contacts, and how a lockout is inserted into trip and close. Asking a one-line to carry the close-permissive contact is the print trap.
reference: Drawing practice; ATS 7.9.1 functional tests still require the contact to perform its scheme job

question: ATS 7.22.1 for an engine generator tells you to verify, as the application requires:
choices: Phase rotation, phasing, and synchronized operation
That synchronization is optional if the breaker is closed fast
explanation: 7.22.1.B.3 and the matching test-value line require phase rotation, phasing, and synchronizing to match the system design. Closing a generator onto a live bus with the wrong rotation is a fault, not a commissioning footnote.

question: A 51 contact energizes an 86 lockout, and an 86 contact energizes the breaker trip coil. In that path, what operates first?
choices: The breaker springs, before any relay
explanation: The 51 has to pick up and close its contact before the 86 coil is energized. The 86 then seals and its contact energizes the trip coil, so the breaker opens third in this particular path. Resetting the breaker does not reset the 86.
reference: Control-schematic sequence; ATS 7.9.1 includes 51 pickup and 86 lockout functional tests

question: An 86 b contact is in the close-permissive string. The lockout trips (coil picked up). That b contact:
choices: Opens and blocks closing until the lockout is reset
Does not change, because b contacts are not used in trip circuits
explanation: A b contact is closed when the device is de-energized and open when the device is picked up. A tripped 86 opens its b contact and removes close permission. An a contact would do the opposite and is the one you would use to energize a trip or an alarm when the lockout operates.

question: ATS 7.9.1’s time-overcurrent (51) test is:
choices: Minimum pickup, and time at two points on the curve
explanation: The 51 list is minimum pickup and time delay at two points on the curve. Slope and harmonic restraint are the 87 list. One point cannot show that the curve is the one in the study.

question: A directional overcurrent (67) test in ATS 7.9.1 includes:
choices: Directional-unit pickup at maximum torque angle, the closing zone, and the overcurrent unit
explanation: Direction is the point of a 67. Pickup at the maximum-torque angle, the zone where the contact closes, and the overcurrent unit all belong in that test. A non-directional 51 will not catch a reversed polarizing circuit.

question: On a microprocessor feeder relay, ATS 7.9.2 says element timing is judged against:
choices: One NETA percent for every relay
explanation: 7.9.2.D.4 says protection elements should operate within the manufacturer’s recommended tolerances. A 50 element and a 51 element on the same relay can have different published bands. Do not borrow Table 100.7 from molded-case breakers.

question: Restoring a relay test switch after injection, the safe order is:
choices: Close the trip poles first so the breaker is protected while CTs are still open
Close the trip poles last, after the current circuits are restored
Leave the CT shorting blade open as a spare
Open the trip poles and go home
explanation: The trip circuit is opened first on the way in, so a stray assertion does not trip, and the CT shorting blade shorts before the current circuit opens. On the way out the trip poles close last, after current is restored. Leaving a CT open under load is the hazard.
reference: Test-switch practice for CT and trip circuits; never open a loaded CT secondary. ATS 7.10.1 requires the secondary to stay a complete circuit.

question: Settings and logic in a microprocessor relay should agree with:
choices: Whatever was found, because changing it is outside testing
The most recent engineered setting file
explanation: ATS 7.9.2 says settings and logic should agree with the latest engineered setting files. As-found that does not match gets written down. As-left is the file, not a dial you liked during the test.

question: A SEL-751-class feeder relay publishes its own pickup and timing tolerances. Those numbers are:
choices: Replaced by a single NETA percent
What you test against for that relay, because 7.9.2 points at the manufacturer
explanation: The percent on the relay manual is that relay’s band. ATS 7.9.2.D.4 tells you to use the manufacturer’s recommended tolerances. Quoting another relay’s ±3% or a breaker’s Table 100.8 is the wrong document.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.D.4; element tolerances per the relay manufacturer

question: Two lockout relays, 86-1 and 86-2, both trip the same breaker and each has a b contact in the close circuit. After a trip, close permissive returns when:
choices: The breaker is closed once, which resets both
explanation: Each b contact is open while its coil is picked up. Series permissives mean both must be reset. Resetting one and closing into the other lockout is how a second trip surprises people.
reference: Control-schematic logic for series 86 b contacts

question: Device 25, synchronism check, in a generator breaker close scheme should:
choices: Close the breaker by itself as soon as frequency is near
Block the close until voltage, angle, and slip are inside the setting
Be defeated for the first parallel
explanation: 25 supervises the close. It does not replace the operator or the 86. ATS 7.22.1 still wants phase rotation, phasing, and synchronizing proved. Bypassing 25 for “the first time” is how out-of-phase closes happen.

question: A close scheme uses an 86 b contact and a 52 b contact in series. The breaker is closed and the lockout is reset. The 52 b contact is:
choices: Closed, because the breaker is closed
Open, because a b contact opens when the breaker is closed
explanation: A b contact is closed only while its device is dropped out. A closed breaker has opened its b contact, which is why that contact is the anti-pump or spring-release permissive and not a seal-in of the close. The 86 b contact is closed only while the lockout is reset.
